subjective.question: What is the cellular concept? Explain the idea of frequency reuse.
subjective.answer: The cellular concept divides the entire service area into small geographic units called cells, each served by its own base station having a subset of the total available channels. Frequencies used in one cell are reused in cells that are sufficiently far away (co-channel cells) so that the interference between them remains within acceptable limits. In this way the limited radio spectrum is reused again and again over the service area, which increases the system capacity many times without requiring additional spectrum.

subjective.question: Define a cluster and cluster size. Calculate the cluster size for i = 1 and j = 2.
subjective.answer: A cluster is a group of cells that collectively uses the complete set of available channels exactly once. The number of cells in a cluster is called the cluster size N, and it is given by N = i^2 + ij + j^2, where i and j are non-negative integers describing the shift between co-channel cells. For i = 1 and j = 2: N = 1 + (1 x 2) + 4 = 7, so the cluster contains 7 cells.

subjective.question: What is co-channel interference? How can it be reduced?
subjective.answer: Co-channel interference is the interference received from cells located in other clusters that use exactly the same set of frequencies. It depends on the reuse distance between co-channel cells and not on the transmitted power alone. It can be reduced by (1) increasing the cluster size, which increases the reuse distance D = R x sqrt(3N), (2) cell sectoring with directional antennas, which reduces the number of interferers seen by a base station, (3) proper frequency planning, and (4) power control.

subjective.question: Differentiate between cell splitting and cell sectoring.
subjective.answer: In cell splitting, a cell that has reached its capacity is divided into smaller cells, each having its own base station with reduced antenna height and transmit power. This adds new channels in the area and increases capacity. In cell sectoring, the cell is not divided; instead the omni-directional antenna at the base station is replaced by directional antennas (for example three 120-degree sectors). Each sector receives signals from only a fraction of the co-channel cells, so the signal-to-interference ratio improves without adding new base stations or channels.

subjective.question: What is trunking? Define Grade of Service (GOS).
subjective.answer: Trunking is the technique in which a small number of channels is shared by a large population of users; a user is assigned any channel that is free at the time of the call. It exploits the fact that all users do not need a channel at the same time, so the channels are utilized efficiently. Grade of Service (GOS) is a measure of the congestion of the system, defined as the probability that a call is blocked (or delayed more than a specified time) during the busiest hour of the day.

subjective.question: What happens to capacity and interference if the cluster size is reduced, for example from 12 to 7?
subjective.answer: If the cluster size is reduced, the total channels are divided among fewer cells, so each cell gets more channels and the capacity per unit area increases. However, the co-channel cells come closer together: the reuse ratio D/R = sqrt(3N) decreases, so the co-channel interference increases and the signal-to-interference ratio falls. Therefore cluster size is chosen as a trade-off: N = 7 is widely used because it gives an SIR of about 18.7 dB (with path-loss exponent 4), just above the 18 dB needed by AMPS.

subjective.question: What is handoff? Describe hard, soft and softer handoff.
subjective.answer: Handoff is the process of transferring an ongoing call from the current cell and channel to a new cell and channel as the mobile moves, without disconnecting the call. In hard handoff (break-before-make) the old connection is released before the new one is established; it is used in GSM. In soft handoff (make-before-break) the mobile remains connected to the old base station while connecting to the new one, and both links carry the call for some time; it is used in CDMA systems. Softer handoff is the same as soft handoff but between two sectors of the same cell, so it is handled at the base station itself.

subjective.question: What is MAHO? Which measurements are involved in it?
subjective.answer: MAHO stands for Mobile Assisted Handoff, used in GSM. In this scheme the mobile station continuously measures the received signal strength and quality of its serving base station as well as the signal strengths of the control channels of the neighbouring base stations. It reports these measurements to the BSC/MSC, and the network decides whether a handoff is needed and to which cell. This distributes the measurement work to the mobiles and results in faster and more reliable handoff decisions.

subjective.question: Which factors must be considered while selecting the signal-strength threshold for handoff initiation?
subjective.answer: The signal-strength threshold for initiating handoff must be chosen carefully. If the threshold is too high, handoffs are initiated too often, even when the serving signal is still usable; this increases signalling load and can cause ping-pong handoffs and unnecessary call drops. If the threshold is too low, the handoff is delayed, the call quality degrades badly and the call may be dropped before the handoff completes. The choice therefore depends on the time required to complete a handoff, the speed of the mobile, the cell size and the propagation environment; a hysteresis margin and averaging of measurements are used to avoid repeated handoffs.

subjective.question: Compare FDMA, TDMA and CDMA multiple access techniques.
subjective.answer: FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access): the available band is divided into separate frequency channels and each user gets one channel for the whole call, e.g. AMPS with 30 kHz channels. TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access): several users share the same carrier frequency in different time slots, e.g. GSM with 8 time slots per 200 kHz carrier. CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access): all users transmit over the same wide band at the same time and are separated by unique spreading codes, e.g. IS-95 and WCDMA; it requires strict power control because of the near-far problem.

subjective.question: Explain the near-far problem in CDMA and how it is solved.
subjective.answer: In CDMA all users share the same frequency band simultaneously. A mobile that is close to the base station arrives with a very strong signal, while a mobile at the cell edge arrives with a weak signal. The strong signal then acts as severe interference and can completely mask the weak signal; this is the near-far problem. It is solved by fast and accurate power control: the base station continuously commands every mobile to adjust its transmit power so that all signals arrive at the base station with almost equal power. In WCDMA this power control runs 1500 times per second.

subjective.question: Describe the GSM network architecture, giving the functions of HLR, VLR, AuC and EIR.
subjective.answer: The mobile station (handset with SIM) communicates with the BTS (Base Transceiver Station), which provides the radio interface. The BSC (Base Station Controller) manages several BTSs, radio resources and handoffs. The MSC (Mobile Switching Centre) performs switching, call setup and mobility management and connects the network to the PSTN. Among the databases: the HLR (Home Location Register) stores the permanent subscriber data and the current location of each subscriber; the VLR (Visitor Location Register) stores temporary data of subscribers currently present in its area; the AuC (Authentication Centre) verifies the subscriber identity and generates ciphering keys; and the EIR (Equipment Identity Register) stores the equipment identities (IMEI) so that stolen or invalid handsets can be blocked.

subjective.question: What is GPRS? How does it differ from circuit-switched data in GSM?
subjective.answer: GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) is a packet-switched data service added on top of the GSM network. Unlike circuit-switched GSM data, where a dedicated channel is reserved for the whole connection even when nothing is being sent, GPRS breaks data into packets and uses the radio channels only when there is data to transfer, so many users share the same channel and charging is by data volume. Two new nodes are added: the SGSN (Serving GPRS Support Node), which tracks the location of mobiles and routes packets within its service area, and the GGSN (Gateway GPRS Support Node), which connects the GPRS network to external packet networks such as the Internet.

subjective.question: Which enhancements does EDGE introduce over GPRS?
subjective.answer: EDGE (Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution) improves GPRS in four ways. (1) It introduces a new modulation, 8-PSK, in addition to GMSK, so each symbol carries 3 bits instead of 1. (2) It defines nine modulation and coding schemes, MCS-1 to MCS-9, instead of the four coding schemes of GPRS. (3) It uses link adaptation: the link adaptation module continuously monitors the propagation condition of the channel and selects the MCS that gives the best throughput. (4) It uses incremental redundancy, in which a failed block is retransmitted with additional parity bits that are combined with the earlier transmission. As a result EDGE gives up to 59.2 kbps per time slot (MCS-9) and 473.6 kbps using all eight slots.

subjective.question: Explain the GSM time slot and frame structure. How does the gross rate of 270.833 kbps arise?
subjective.answer: In GSM each 200 kHz carrier is shared in time by eight users. The carrier is divided into TDMA frames of 4.615 ms duration, and each frame contains 8 time slots of about 0.577 ms. Each time slot carries 156.25 bits, so the gross rate of the carrier is 156.25 bits / 0.577 ms, which is approximately 270.833 kbps. Every mobile is assigned one slot in each frame; after coding, this provides a 13 kbps full-rate speech channel per user.

subjective.question: List the key radio parameters of WCDMA.
subjective.answer: The main radio parameters of WCDMA are: chip rate 3.84 Mcps; channel (carrier) bandwidth 5 MHz; frame duration 10 ms divided into 15 slots; fast closed-loop power control at 1500 Hz; variable spreading factor, which allows multi-rate services (from low-rate voice to 2 Mbps data); and support for soft and softer handover. WCDMA was selected as the radio access technology for UMTS and its first major milestone, Release 99, was completed in 1999.

subjective.question: What is spreading in WCDMA? Define processing gain.
subjective.answer: Spreading means that the narrowband data signal of a user is multiplied by a wideband pseudo-noise (chipping) sequence running at 3.84 Mcps, so the signal energy is spread over the whole 5 MHz channel. At the receiver, the signal is correlated with the same code, which despreads the wanted signal while the signals of other users remain spread and appear as low-level noise. Processing gain is the ratio of the chip rate to the user data rate, Gp = Rc / Rb. A larger processing gain gives better protection against interference and allows more users to share the band.

subjective.question: What is HSDPA? On which factors does its performance depend?
subjective.answer: HSDPA (High-Speed Downlink Packet Access), introduced in 3GPP Release 5, is an enhancement of UMTS that raises the downlink data rate to a theoretical peak of 14.4 Mbps. It uses adaptive modulation and coding (QPSK and 16-QAM), fast scheduling performed at the Node B every 2 ms, and fast hybrid ARQ. The performance of HSDPA depends on the channel conditions, the performance of the terminal, and the nature and accuracy of the radio resource management.

subjective.question: Compare 1G, 2G, 2.5G and 3G cellular systems.
subjective.answer: 1G systems (e.g. AMPS) used analog transmission with FDMA and provided only voice service. 2G systems (e.g. GSM, IS-95) used digital transmission, provided better voice quality, SMS and low-rate circuit-switched data of about 9.6 kbps. 2.5G systems (GPRS and EDGE) added packet-switched data, reaching about 171.2 kbps (GPRS) and 473.6 kbps (EDGE). 3G systems (UMTS/WCDMA and cdma2000) follow the IMT-2000 requirements of 144 kbps for high-mobility users, 384 kbps for pedestrians and 2 Mbps for indoor users, and support multimedia services.

subjective.question: What is the difference between path loss and multipath fading?
subjective.answer: Path loss is a large-scale effect: it is the average reduction in signal power as the distance between transmitter and receiver increases, and it also grows with frequency. It changes slowly and is described by the path-loss exponent of the environment. Multipath fading is a small-scale effect: the signal reaches the receiver through many reflected paths, and these copies add constructively or destructively, causing rapid fluctuations of the received signal over distances of a fraction of a wavelength. When there is no line-of-sight path, this fading follows the Rayleigh distribution.
